📝 Exam
Language traps + equations · {0} questions
Excellent! One last exam: language traps. Pick the correct wording — in the quantum world many mistakes are made with words, not with calculations.

Level complete! Rating: {0} (mistakes: {1}, difficulty: {2}).
You will find new cards in the Codex (key C).
You are playing ∑ Equation Language (Experimental). At the top of the screen you will see the real equation that holds right now — its values change when you do something.
The symbols in the equations are drawn as small pictures — glyphs. Hover over one and its tooltip tells you what it means. You will find all of them under the 🔑 key in the top right.
Before every task I will first show you its equation (the ∑ card) and only then the picture.

Hi! Welcome to Hilbert Island. I am Spark — a little spark of light that will guide you around the island. (Don’t mix me up with the amplitude symbol — that one has a magnitude and a phase, I just glow.)

And you are Little Psi — the quantum state ψ. You are not a little ball with a position and a velocity. You are a rule for predictions: you tell what outcomes anyone who asks you something (measures you) will get.
See that golden hand turning around you? That is your global phase. It turns, but nobody in the world can measure it. Remember: the global phase is unobservable, the relative phase is not.

There are 11 portals with mentors around the island — Euler, Stern, Bloch, Feynman, Dirac, Rabi, Bell, Bohr, Pauli, von Neumann and Born — plus the NMR Workshop with Edward Purcell, open from the start. They will teach you the language, the symbols and the right pictures of the quantum world.
Above the island circles Ketvarr, the quantum dragon. Each mentor will teach you one Word of Power. Once you have all eleven, climb Dragon’s Peak in the north and defeat him.
The goal is not to compute integrals. The goal is intuition: knowing what an amplitude is, what a probability is, what a measurement does and where classical analogies stop working.
Controls: WASD move, mouse drag camera, E enter/talk, C Codex of symbols, M map, H help. Start with portal 1!

You are playing the Equation Language (Experimental) type, so the ring has an extra portal 0 — the Hall of Symbols. It introduces the symbols you will meet in the equations and what they mean; I suggest starting there.
New to the quantum world? Switch the difficulty (top right) to 🫶 Layman — I will explain everything in everyday words.

One more thing: the island is full of classical misconceptions. Fight them with spells 1–7 (Tab = target, right-click = attack), gather experience and money, shop at Planck’s by the fountain (B = bags). Talk to me again and I will give you your first quest.
. Don’t forget: amplitudes interfere, probabilities are only measured.
The meadows beyond the portals are crawling with Hidden Variables. They whisper that the outcome was fixed in advance.
Bell proved that no local hidden variables can explain quantum correlations. Debunk 5 of them — and come back to me.
Well done. Remember: quantum probabilities are not just our ignorance.
Billiard-Ball Electrons roll around the island as if they had a definite path.
Between measurements a quantum object has no trajectory. Break 6 of them.
A path is a picture from classical physics. You have a better one: the state and its amplitudes.
The Little-Planet Atoms claim electrons orbit the nucleus like planets around the Sun.
Such an electron would radiate and fall into the nucleus within a hundredth of a billionth of a second. Bring down 4.
An orbital is not a path but a distribution of amplitudes. Exactly.
Faster-than-Light Signals fly over the bridge, promising messages faster than light.
Entanglement gives correlations, not messages — Bob’s statistics don’t depend on Alice’s choice. Intercept 4.
No-signalling holds. Relativity breathes a sigh of relief.
“Dead-and-alive” cats haunt the edge of the island.
A superposition is not “both at once” — the state gives probabilities, a measurement one outcome. Calm 4.
Schrödinger would be pleased. His cat was a critique, not a recipe.
The Consciousness Cultists preach that the world collapses only when someone looks.
A measurement is a physical interaction; decoherence runs even in an empty lab. Disperse 5.
The island is clean of misconceptions. You are a true quantum mage.
Welcome to the Complex Harbour! I am Leonhard Euler. I introduced the letters e and i — and in quantum mechanics you will see them at every step.
An analogy: an amplitude is like the hand of a clock. It has a length (magnitude) and an angle (phase). In the quantum world every possible outcome carries such a hand.
The probability is the square of the length of the hand: |α|². It doesn’t care about the angle at all! So why does phase exist? You’ll find out in the third task. 😉
Beneath you is the complex plane: horizontally Re (real part), vertically Im (imaginary part). The circle is the unit circle.
Exactly! Notice: while you changed only the phase, the probability bar didn’t move. It changed only when you changed the magnitude.
Two amplitudes: 0.7 and [[0.7·e<sup>iπ/2</sup> (= 0.7i)]]. Do they have the same probability?
Yes, both 0.49
No, the second has −0.49
No, the second has 0.7
[[|0.7i|² = 0.7i · (−0.7i) = 0.49]]. The phase is lost in |α|².
Done in {0} presses. Multiplying by i = rotating by 90°. Two rotations = 180°, so [[i · i = i² = −1]]. No magic, just geometry!
And one more thing: [[eiπ = −1]]. The phase π (a 180° rotation) is exactly the minus sign that distinguishes the states |+⟩ and |−⟩. You will meet them in the Bloch Observatory.
How many times must we multiply the number 1 by i to get to −i?
3 times (270°)
once
4 times
[[1 → i → −1 → −i]]. Four presses would bring us back to 1.
Now the most important part. Two paths lead to the same outcome, each with its own amplitude A₁ and A₂ (length 0.5).

The quantum rule: first add the hands (amplitudes), only then square: [[P = |A₁ + A₂|²]]. The classical rule for mutually exclusive alternatives would add probabilities: [[|A₁|² + |A₂|² = 0.5]] always.
An analogy: two people push a swing. If they push in rhythm, the swing flies high. If they push against each other, it doesn’t move. What matters is the rhythm — the relative phase.
Excellent! At phase [[π, P = 0]], even though each path alone would give ¼. This is the core of quantum mechanics: the phase is invisible in a single amplitude, but it decides when amplitudes meet.
Quantum algorithms do exactly this: they arrange the phases so that wrong answers cancel and right ones are reinforced.
Otto Stern
Welcome to Frankfurt, 1922! Silver atoms fly out of this furnace. Each has one unpaired electron, and it behaves like a tiny magnet.
Walther Gerlach
We send the beam through an inhomogeneous magnetic field (the top pole is sharp, the bottom one flat). Depending on its orientation, the magnetic moment is deflected up or down.
Otto Stern
The classical picture: the little magnets point in random directions → a continuous band should appear on the screen. Let’s test it!
How many spots does the real (quantum) beam make on the screen?
two separate spots
a continuous band
one spot in the middle
Measuring the projection of a spin ½ along a chosen axis has only two outcomes: +ħ/2 and −ħ/2.
Walther Gerlach
We call the upper spot [[Sz = +ħ/2]] (state [[|0⟩ ≡ |+z⟩]], “spin up”), the lower one [[Sz = −ħ/2]] (state [[|1⟩ ≡ |−z⟩]]).
Otto Stern

Mind the language! The experiment did not show how the electron spins. It showed what outcomes a precisely specified measurement gives. And “spin ½” doesn’t mean half a turn — it is the name of a kind of quantum spin.
Otto Stern
Now you can chain up to three magnets, rotate them (z axis = 0°, x axis = 90°) and set a filter that lets only one beam through.
Walther Gerlach
Setup A: the first Z magnet lets only “+” through, the second magnet measures Z again. Setup B: put an X magnet (passing “+”) between them. Guess the result before you fire!
Why does setup [[B (Z+ → X+ → Z)]] give 50 : 50 again at the end?
The x measurement prepared a new state |+x⟩; in it the z outcome is uncertain.
The X magnet damaged the atoms.
The atoms had hidden values for all axes and the X magnet shuffled them.
Certainty in one basis does not mean certainty in another. The measurement basis is part of the question. Spin is not an arrow with predetermined values for x, y and z all at once.
The atoms passed a “+z” filter. The second magnet is rotated {0}° from the z axis. What fraction goes to its upper spot?
The probability is [[cos²({0}°/2) = {1}]]. On the Bloch sphere: (1 + cos {0}°)/2. The smaller the angle between the axes, the more certain the outcome.
Otto Stern

We measured {0} up (theory {1}). A single measurement always gives just +ħ/2 or −ħ/2, but the statistics of many repetitions reveal the probability. That is exactly how the Born rule is tested in the lab.
X = a 180° rotation about the x axis. From the north pole to the south: quantum NOT, a “bit flip”. Notice: |0⟩ and |1⟩ are perpendicular in Hilbert space but antipodal on the Bloch sphere.

H rotates about the axis between x and z → swaps the axes [[z ↔ x]]. Mind the language: H “creates a superposition” only from the point of view of the Z basis. Applied to |+⟩ it would “undo” one instead.
Look at P(0) and P(1): they didn’t change (still ½ and ½)! Z changed only the relative phase by π. Indistinguishable in the Z basis, completely different states in the X basis.
H brought you down to the equator [[(θ = π/2), S]] turned the phase by [[π/2 (φ = π/2)]]. Two angles θ and φ are enough to describe any pure qubit.
[[H·Z·H = X]]. Different sequences of rotations can give the same overall rotation. Every gate is unitary = a rotation that preserves the length of the arrow.

Look at the notation: [[Y|0⟩ = i|1⟩]]. The factor i is a global phase — the same for the whole state, impossible to measure. That’s why we write [[i|1⟩ ∼ |1⟩]] (“equal up to a global phase”). The arrow on the sphere is the same!
E.g. [[H → |+⟩, S → |+i⟩, Z → |−i⟩]] (or H, Z, S). Relative phase [[φ = 3π/2]] — that is −i. Different paths over the sphere, the same target.
[[T·T = S]]: two 45° rotations about z make 90°. The phase gates form a ladder: [[T² = S, S² = Z]].
Grüezi! I am Felix Bloch. Thanks to NMR I showed that the state of a spin can be drawn as an arrow in a ball. Today we call it the Bloch sphere.

An analogy: the Bloch sphere is a globe of states. North pole = |0⟩, south = |1⟩, the equator = equal superpositions. Latitude (the angle θ) sets the measurement probabilities in the Z basis, longitude (φ) is the relative phase.
But careful: this is not a map of the laboratory, and the arrow is not the axis of a spinning ball! It is a picture of the amplitudes α and β.
Gates are rotations of this ball. Solve {0} puzzles: bring the (red) arrow onto the golden target with a limited set of gates. You can rotate the ball with the mouse.
The states |+⟩ and |−⟩ have the same [[P(0) = P(1) = ½]]. Are they the same state?
No — they differ by a relative phase, and a measurement in the X basis tells them apart with certainty
Yes — same probabilities = same state
Yes, they differ only by a global phase
Equal statistics in one basis do not mean the same state. They are even orthogonal!
The last lesson: measurement. The arrow holds a lot of information (both θ and φ). How much of it do you get from one measurement?
Click Measure 1× on the state |+⟩. Then Measure 100 copies — the same preparations, independent measurements.
What did ONE measurement of the qubit give us?
one bit (0 or 1), and the state changed to |0⟩ or |1⟩
the values of α and β
the angles θ and φ

One measurement = one bit. You learn the probabilities only from the statistics of many identically prepared copies. And the phase φ only by measuring in another basis. (Try it: |+⟩ and |+i⟩ give the same statistics in the Z basis!)
Finally, a free lab. Every pure state is a point (θ, φ), every gate is a rotation Rn(α) about some axis n, and every measurement is the question “is the state along m?” — [[P(+m) = (1 + r·m)/2]].
Hey! I’m Dick Feynman. I once said the double-slit experiment contains the only mystery of quantum mechanics. Here is its qubit version.
The track: the qubit starts in |0⟩, passes through gate H, the centre of the temple and a second gate H. At the end a detector measures it: 0 or 1.

An analogy: two paths lead to the treasure. As long as nobody knows which one you took, their amplitudes can add up or cancel. Once someone finds out (measures), the interference disappears — only ordinary probabilities remain.
At the back you see the density matrix ρ (rho) as bars: the two on the diagonal = probabilities (populations), the two off the diagonal = coherences, the “memory of the phase”.
Qubit [[|0⟩ → H → H]] → measurement. What do you measure?
always 0
always 1
[[H·H = I]]. The contributions to |1⟩ cancel destructively, those to |0⟩ add up constructively.
Now we put a Z-basis measurement in the centre and FORGET its result. What do you measure at the end?
always 0
always 1
The measurement destroys the coherence (off-diagonal elements of ρ). What remains is the mixture [[½|0⟩⟨0| + ½|1⟩⟨1| = I/2]] — and the second H doesn’t change it.
A measurement is the extreme case. In a real chip the qubit slowly “leaks” into the environment: decoherence. It is as if the environment partly measured the phase.
Use the slider to set the decoherence strength p (0 = nothing, 1 = a full measurement). Task: find p for which [[P(0) = {0}]], and send at least {1} qubits.
Also new: a phase shifter φ in the centre of the temple (a rotation about the z axis). It decides whether the paths meet “in rhythm” — interference fringes: [[P(0) = (1 + (1 − p)·cos φ)/2]].
See? Always 0. Look at ρ along the way: after the first H all four bars are equally tall — the off-diagonal coherences carry the phase information, and the second H turns it into certainty.

After the measurement the off-diagonal bars vanished. The diagonal is the same as for the superposition (½, ½), so a measurement in the Z basis cannot tell them apart. The difference shows only in the next operation.
On the Bloch sphere: the arrow shrank to the centre (the maximally mixed state I/2). The second H rotates the ball, but a point at the centre does not move under rotation.
Exactly: [[p = {0}]] shrinks the coherences to {1} and [[P(0) = (1 + (1 − p)·cos φ)/2 = {2}]]. The arrow is shorter than 1 → a mixed state inside the ball.
Mathematically, the second gate acts on the density matrix as HρH† (the dagger † = Hermitian conjugate). For the mixture I/2 you get I/2 again — nothing changes.
The lesson for quantum computers: coherence is the fuel of interference. Lose it and you lose the advantage.
⟨a|ψ⟩ — the bra “asks the question” (is it state a?), the ket is the answer. Together they give a number: the amplitude. Bra-ket = “bracket”.
|⟨a|ψ⟩|² — the Born rule. The amplitude is theory, the probability is experiment.
|ψ⟩⟨ψ| — column times row = a matrix. The same symbols as in ⟨ψ|ψ⟩, the opposite order, a completely different object!
⟨ψ|Â|ψ⟩ — the average of many measurements. Careful: it need not be a value you can get in a single run!
Ĥ|ψ⟩ — the operator “processes” a ket and returns a ket. An operator acts to the right, on a ket.
⟨φ|Â|ψ⟩ — a complex number, an element of the matrix. Read from the right: Â acts on ψ, the result is projected onto φ.
|ψ⟩ ⊗ |φ⟩ — the tensor product. For two qubits [[|0⟩ ⊗ |1⟩ = |01⟩]]. Dimensions multiply: 2 × 2 = 4 amplitudes.
Dirac.
Librarian Ket
(whispering) Professor Dirac is famously taciturn. His colleagues supposedly introduced the unit 1 dirac = one word per hour. Allow me to interpret.
Librarian Ket

The professor invented the bra-ket notation — the grammar of quantum mechanics. Every expression has a type, just as a word in a language has a part of speech: ket |ψ⟩ = state (column), bra ⟨ψ| = question (row), Â = operator (machine).
Librarian Ket

An analogy: a ket is a letter, a bra is an addressed envelope. Put the letter into the envelope — ⟨a|ψ⟩ — and you get a number (a stamp, an amplitude). Put them the other way round, |ψ⟩⟨a|, and you get a machine (an operator) that turns letters into other letters.
Librarian Ket
On the table (3D) you will see shapes: arrow = ket, plank = bra, cube = operator, coin = number, bar = probability. Put tokens together and learn what comes out of what.
Correct.
Librarian Ket
Which expression is an OPERATOR?
⟨φ|ψ⟩
⟨ψ|Â|ψ⟩
Ket-bra = operator; bra-ket = number; ⟨ψ|Â|ψ⟩ = number (expectation value).
Good.
Librarian Ket
(From him that is almost an ode!) The main idea: |ψ⟩ is an abstract state, and [[ψ(x) = ⟨x|ψ⟩]] is just its “coordinate” in the position basis — just like [[cn = ⟨n|ψ⟩]] in a discrete basis.
Shalom! I am I. I. Rabi. In 1938 I taught atoms to “listen to the radio” — that is magnetic resonance. From it came NMR, MRI and atomic clocks.
Pieter Zeeman
Allow me to add: in a static field B₀ the energy of a spin ½ splits into two levels (the Zeeman effect). Those two levels are our qubit.

On the left is the NMR magnet with a sample (e.g. dimethyl phosphite molecules in a SpinQ). On the right is the Bloch sphere of the nuclear spin. Down in the panel there is a plot: P(|1⟩) and the NMR signal.
An analogy: an RF pulse is like pushing a swing: if you push in the right rhythm (resonance), the swing goes all the way. Out of rhythm it only wobbles a bit.
In the laboratory frame the arrow circled around the z axis (precession). Did the probability P(|1⟩) change meanwhile?
No — precession changes only the relative phase φ, not θ
Yes, it oscillated
Yes, it kept growing
Look at the plot: the green line is flat, only the orange signal oscillates. Precession ≠ gyroscope: it is the evolution of the phase between |0⟩ and |1⟩.

In the rotating frame we turn together with the spin (at the Larmor frequency), so the fast precession “stops”. It is a mathematical trick — the laboratory does not rotate. From now on we will work in this frame.
That is a π pulse: a 180° rotation — like the X gate. The pulse area ΩR·t is the rotation angle, not a time in seconds.
If you made the pulse longer, the state would come back: those are Rabi oscillations. It is the probability that oscillates, not an electron between two places!
A π/2 pulse — an equal superposition. In NMR it is the basic step of almost every experiment.
Someone has moved the frequency of the RF generator. Off resonance the spin rotates about a tilted axis and never fully flips. Find the rhythm of the swing!
Resonance found! This is exactly how the frequency of a nucleus is found in NMR. The frequency difference (detuning) tilts the rotation axis.

Real spins feel their neighbours and field inhomogeneities. Each molecule precesses a little differently and the phases drift apart: T₂ (dephasing). The slower return of populations to the thermal state is T₁.
The arrow has shrunk towards the axis — a mixed state (|r| < 1). Meanwhile the orange NMR signal faded: that is the FID (free induction decay).
In NMR (e.g. SpinQ) we do not measure a single spin but an ensemble of ~10²⁰ molecules. The signal is the expectation value of the transverse magnetisation, not individual 0/1 outcomes.
Good day, I am John Bell from CERN. Welcome to the bridge of entanglement. On the left stands Alice with her qubit, on the right Bob.

And I am Einstein. In 1935, with Podolsky and Rosen, we argued that quantum mechanics is incomplete. If I can predict something at a distance with certainty, it must be an “element of reality” beforehand! No spukhafte Fernwirkung — spooky action at a distance.
In 1964 I showed how this dispute can be settled by experiment. But first you have to make an entangled pair.
Excellent! Now look at the Bloch spheres: both arrows vanished into the centre.

The whole |Φ⁺⟩ is a pure state, but neither qubit on its own has a state of its own — each is maximally mixed. The information is neither “in Alice” nor “in Bob”, it is in the correlations. That is entanglement: the whole is more than the sum of its parts.
With Z–Z the outcomes are always the same! I told you: the values must have been fixed in advance, like two gloves in two boxes.

Perhaps. But look at Bob: whether Alice measures Z or X, Bob sees 50 : 50 every time. This way Alice cannot send him a message — they see the correlations only after comparing results over an ordinary (classical, slower) channel.
And a game will decide about the gloves. Let’s go!
The rules of the CHSH game: the referee sends Alice a random bit x and Bob a random bit y. Without communicating, they answer with bits a, b.
They win if a ⊕ [[b = x · y]]: so they should answer the same, except when [[x = y = 1]], when they should answer differently.
If they have “gloves” — answers agreed in advance (local hidden variables) — they never exceed 75 %. That is Bell’s inequality.
With an entangled pair, Alice picks the measurement angle a₀ or a₁ depending on x, and Bob picks b₀ or b₁ depending on y. Try to find angles that beat 75 %!
{0}! The theoretical maximum is [[cos²(π/8) ≈ 85 %]]. No gloves can do this.
Hmm... So either I give up locality, or the idea that values exist before the measurement.

Exactly. Bohm chooses non-locality (the pilot wave), the operational approach (Bohr) gives up pre-existing values. And note: you still haven’t sent each other a message. Aspect, Clauser and Zeilinger received the 2022 Nobel Prize for the experimental confirmation.
Velkommen! I am Niels Bohr. My coat of arms bears the yin-yang and the motto Contraria sunt complementa — opposites are complementary.
A physicist must be able to calculate. But he must also be able to speak — and not speak nonsense. In this hall stand the thinkers your lectures mention.

Complementarity: a quantum object cannot be described by a single classical picture. Wave and particle are both precise descriptions, each within its own experimental arrangement. This is not relativism!
Talk to all six of them. Each will ask you a question.
Excellent. The lecture warns you: don’t mix up three questions — ontology (What exists?), epistemology (What can we know about it?), phenomenology (How does the phenomenon appear to us?).
Classify the following sentences.
Niels Bohr
“Is the wave function ψ physical reality, or just a tool for prediction?” — What kind of question is this?
ontological
epistemological
phenomenological
It asks what exists. Neither the Schrödinger equation nor experiments settle this dispute by themselves.
Niels Bohr
“What can we know at the same time about the position and momentum of an electron?”
epistemological
ontological
phenomenological
A question about the limits of knowledge.
Niels Bohr
“How does spin appear to us in the Stern–Gerlach experiment — two spots on the screen?”
phenomenological
ontological
epistemological
A question about how a phenomenon appears in experience/experiment.
Niels Bohr
Which of these is NOT one of the “four questions” to ask about every new quantum concept?
Which observer is right?
What system have we prepared?
In what experiment do the properties show up?
What does this description still NOT imply?
The four questions: the system, the equation and assumptions, the experiment, and what does (not) follow from the description.
“There is no need to stop calculating the world. What we must not forget is what kind of world it is that we are calculating.” — so ends the lecture on the language of quantum mechanics.
The dragon has P(hit) = 70 %. You struck and missed. What happened?
The measurement gave the less likely outcome — 30 % happens too; the ward collapsed onto the opposite pole
The probability was computed wrongly
The dragon noticed you measuring and changed the angle
The Born rule gives probabilities, not certainties. After a measurement the state is in one of the two outcomes.
Why did the “Phase Hiss” (a rotation about z) not hurt you while you stood at |1⟩?
The poles are eigenstates of Z — a rotation about z changes them only by a global phase
Because the dragon missed
Because |1⟩ is the zero vector
[[Rz(φ)|1⟩ = e<sup>iφ/2</sup>|1⟩]] — a global phase is unobservable.
The Fog of Decoherence shrank the ward’s arrow to length 0.5. What is the highest P(hit) you can reach with gates alone?
75 % — rotations do not lengthen the arrow: [[P ≤ (1 + |r|)/2]]
100 % — you just need the right gate
Unitary gates are rotations; a mixed state stays mixed. Only a measurement (collapse) helps — or not letting the fog catch you on the equator.
So you have passed through all eleven portals. I am Erwin Schrödinger — yes, the one with the cat. On this mountain peak nests Ketvarr, the quantum dragon.
His scales are guarded by a ward that is a qubit. You see it on the right as a Bloch ball. The golden arrow n is his weak spot.

Your sword is measurement. A strike hits with probability [[P = (1 + r·n)/2]] — the closer the ward’s arrow is to the golden one, the surer the hit. And beware: after a strike the ward collapses onto one of the poles.
Don’t say the dragon is “in the sky and on the ground at once”. Say it precisely: he is in a state that gives P(hit). The two translucent dragons only show the probabilities of the outcomes.

The fight is turn-based: you shout one Word of Power (a gate), then the dragon makes an announced move and breathes fire. Only a strike with [[P ≥ {0}]] wounds Ketvarr — that is the metric you must hit.
🐉 Ketvarr: “A little state ψ wants to measure a dragon? My scales are made of stone and phases!”

Schrödinger: His moves in round 1 are mostly rotations about z. Those don’t move the poles… and now and then a Wing Flip (X). Watch the announced move and the numbers on the buttons — they show P(hit) after the dragon’s move.
🐉 Ketvarr: “Fog! Let your coherence dissolve!”
Schrödinger: Now he breathes the Fog of Decoherence, which shrinks the arrow on the equator. You have learned a new word: RABI-RA — a pulse with an adjustable angle θ. Don’t linger on the equator!
🐉 Ketvarr: “My heart is not where you seek it!”
Schrödinger: The weak spot n is now tilted, and the dragon moves it. The pulse also has an axis φ in the equatorial plane. Aim so that after the dragon’s move P ≥ the threshold.
Ketvarr
Ketvarr roars and his stone scales crack! “The poles… you stood on the poles, where my phase can do nothing!”
Well done. Rotations about z change only the phase — at the poles |0⟩, |1⟩ they are harmless.
The fog parts. “My fog… you did not linger on the equator!”
Exactly. Decoherence destroys coherences — the arrow on the equator. A quick pulse and a measurement beat it.
Ketvarr falls into the snow. “You aimed at my heart… even though it moved.”
This is quantum control in miniature: predict the evolution and tune the pulse so that the outcome has a high probability.
Ketvarr
Ketvarr
“Ashes to ashes, amplitude to zero!”
The fire overwhelmed you. No matter — the round starts over. Tip: look at the numbers on the buttons and the dragon’s announced move before you shout.
Ketvarr is defeated. Three more questions — I want to know whether you understand why you won.
Ketvarr
“Very well, little state. Nobody has ever measured me so precisely. I will fly to the northern peak and guard the island — against bad analogies.”

🏆 Hilbert Island is saved! Battle rating: {0} (mistakes: {1}).
Remember: amplitudes interfere, probabilities are measured, and the dragon is in a state — not “in two places at once”.
Hi! I am Spark, your guide. I will explain everything in everyday words.
Ordinary computers use bits: each is 0 or 1. Quantum computers use qubits: until you look at one, a qubit can be a blend of 0 and 1.
You are Little Psi (ψ) — the state of a qubit. You are not a little ball but a recipe for chances: you say what answers anyone who looks at you will get.
The trick of quantum computers: every possible answer carries a little arrow. Arrows can cancel each other out. A good quantum program makes the wrong answers cancel and the right one grow.
Above the island circles Ketvarr, the quantum dragon. Each mentor teaches you one Word of Power; with all eleven you will defeat him on Dragon’s Peak.

There are 11 portals with mentors on the island and an NMR Workshop where you try out a real machine. Before every task I will first explain it in plain words. Technical words get a translation in brackets and a simple explanation when you hover them.
Controls: WASD move, mouse drag camera, E enter/talk, M map. Start with portal 1!
Once you feel more confident, you can switch to a harder difficulty with more technical language at any time (top right).
In a quantum computer every possible answer carries a little arrow (like a clock hand).
Long arrow = a likely answer. Short arrow = an unlikely one. The arrow’s direction (its “phase”) is like timing — it only matters when arrows meet.
Simple task: drag the arrow onto the golden mark — the right length and the right direction. That’s all “setting an amplitude” means.
The “× i” button just turns the arrow a quarter turn (90°) and keeps its length. Two quarter turns = the arrow points backwards.
Two routes lead to the same answer, and each brings its own arrow. The arrows add up tip to tail.
Same direction → they team up (a surer answer). Opposite directions → they cancel (that answer can’t happen). This is exactly how quantum computers win: wrong answers cancel, the right one grows.
Atoms behave like tiny magnets. We send them through a big magnet and look where they land.
Everyday experience says: a smeared stripe. Reality says: only two spots — “up” or “down”. That “always one of two answers” property is exactly a qubit (a quantum bit).
First fire in the “classical” model (how it would work by everyday intuition), then in reality. Compare: a stripe vs. two dots.
A filter = we ask a question and keep only one answer. Ask “up/down?”, then “left/right?”, then “up/down?” again.
Surprise: the middle question wipes out the first answer. In the quantum world asking a question changes what you ask about.
A tilted magnet = a slightly different question. The more it’s tilted, the more the answer becomes a coin toss (50/50). Guess first, then fire.
Picture a qubit as an arrow inside a ball. North pole = 0, south pole = 1, anywhere else = a blend of 0 and 1.
Gates (the operations of a quantum computer) just turn this arrow. A quantum program = a sequence of turns.

Each puzzle: get the arrow to the target with as few buttons as possible. X swaps top ↔ bottom, H swaps the north pole with a point on the equator, Z turns the arrow half a turn around the vertical axis.
Measuring = asking the qubit “are you 0 or 1?”. An arrow on the equator answers randomly, 50/50. The arrow then jumps to the pole of the answer.
One try tells you almost nothing; a hundred tries show the pattern. Real quantum computers also run the same program many times.
Free play: point the arrow anywhere, turn it and measure in any direction. Nothing can go wrong here.
There are two kinds of “not sure”: a genuine blend that can still interfere (superposition), and a coin someone already tossed but hasn’t shown you (a mixture).
In a single measurement they look the same. The difference shows when you do one more step before measuring.
H twice in a row always brings the qubit back to 0 — the two routes to the answer 1 cancel each other. That’s interference at work.
Peek in the middle and the magic is gone: suddenly it’s 50/50 at the end. Looking (or any leak of information) destroys the interference.
The ρ bars off the diagonal are “the blend is still alive” indicators. Watch them go dark.
Decoherence = the surroundings peeking a little. More noise → less interference. It is enemy no. 1 of real quantum computers — that’s why they are cooled almost to absolute zero.
Dirac’s notation is just shorthand. |ψ⟩ (a “ket”) = a state, like a noun. ⟨φ| (a “bra”) = a question you ask.
⟨φ|ψ⟩ = the answer to the question: a single number (an arrow). Its length squared = the chance.
Build expressions from tiles like LEGO. Always ask: is the result a state, a number, or a machine that changes states?
NMR is the technique behind the MRI scanner in a hospital — and behind the first quantum computers, too.
A strong magnet gives every atomic nucleus two energy levels (= 0 and 1). Radio pulses of the right tone switch it between them.
In the magnet the arrow spins like a top. From the lab it looks busy; from a merry-go-round turning with it (the rotating frame) it stands still.
While it spins, the chances of 0 and 1 don’t change.
A π pulse = a radio pulse just long enough to flip 0 into 1. It is the quantum NOT gate.
A pulse half as long stops halfway: a 50/50 blend. That’s how superposition is made on real hardware.
Like tuning a radio: the wrong frequency and the flip doesn’t work. Find the right station.
Leave the blend alone and it fades — the nuclei drift out of step. T₂ = how long the qubit “remembers”. A quantum computation must finish before that.
Entanglement: two qubits share one joint state. Their results are linked — always equal, for example — even when they are far apart.
Einstein called it “spooky”. Bell figured out how to test it by experiment.
Recipe: H on the first qubit (make it a 50/50 blend), then CNOT (flip the second one if the first is 1). Done — they’re entangled.
Bob on his own always sees a fair coin, whatever Alice does. So entanglement cannot send a message faster than light — the link only shows up when they compare notes.
A cooperation game: Alice and Bob can’t talk, but they can share entangled pairs. With ordinary strategies they win at most 75 % of rounds, with entanglement about 85 %.
Tilt the measurement angles until you beat 75 %.
The finale! The dragon Ketvarr has a ward that is a qubit — the arrow in the ball on the right. Your sword is measurement: you strike and either hit or miss.

The chance of a hit grows the closer the ward’s arrow points to the golden arrow. It’s turn-based: you say one word (a turn of the arrow), then the dragon makes one move, which he announces in advance.
The numbers on the buttons show the chance of a hit next turn — already including the dragon’s move. Just pick whatever is green, then strike.
Now the dragon blows fog that shortens the arrow on the equator — a shorter arrow = worse aim. At the poles the fog does no harm. The new slider θ sets how far you turn the arrow.
The golden arrow (the dragon’s heart) is tilted and the dragon moves it. Adjust the θ and φ sliders until the pulse button turns green — then shout it and strike next turn.
No more knobs — this level is about what the theory means. Physicists agree on the maths and the predictions but still argue about what is “really” going on.
Chat with six thinkers. Each sees it differently, and you don’t have to pick a winner.
Sort questions into three piles: what exists? (being), what can we know? (knowing), what do we see and experience? (experience).
The final quiz tests words, not sums. Tip: chance = arrow length squared; arrows add up, chances don’t. The trap is usually an everyday word used in the wrong place.

The square root of a negative number

In Ars Magna (1545), solving “divide 10 into two parts whose product is 40”, Cardano obtained 5 ± √−15. The result worked, but he did not know what it meant. Bombelli, in L’Algebra (1572), was the first to give rules for calculating with “più di meno” (today’s +i) and “meno di meno” (−i) — and showed that they lead to perfectly real roots of cubic equations.
“So progresses arithmetic subtlety, the end of which, as is said, is as refined as it is useless.” — Cardano on √−15
“Imaginary” and Euler’s formula

In La Géométrie (1637) Descartes called these roots, dismissively, “imaginary” — and the name stuck. In Introductio in analysin infinitorum (1748) Euler published [[eix = cos x + i sin x]], and in 1777 he introduced the letter i for √−1. Already in a letter to Goldbach (1746) he had computed that ii is a real number ≈ 0.2079.
“Our jewel … the most remarkable formula in mathematics.” — Richard Feynman on [[e<sup>iθ</sup> = cos θ + i sin θ]] (The Feynman Lectures, 1963)
Numbers as arrows, probability as a square

The surveyor Wessel (1799) and the bookkeeper Argand (1806) independently drew complex numbers as points of a plane — multiplication became rotation. Gauss (1831) gave them the name “complex”. In 1926 Max Born added in a footnote of a paper on collisions that the probability is proportional to the square of the amplitude — today’s Born rule (Nobel Prize 1954).
“The motion of particles follows probability laws but the probability itself propagates according to the law of causality.” — Max Born, 1926
A postcard to Bohr

Stern proposed the experiment in 1921, aiming to disprove Bohr’s “space quantisation”. After months of failure, Gerlach in Frankfurt saw, in February 1922, the deposit on the glass plate split in two. He sent Bohr a postcard with a micrograph of the two spots. (Only later did it turn out that the effect was not orbital angular momentum but electron spin.)
“Attached is the experimental proof of directional quantisation. We congratulate you on the confirmation of your theory.” — Gerlach to Bohr, 8 Feb 1922
A cheap cigar

The silver layer on the plate was so thin that it could not be seen. According to Stern’s recollection, the trace appeared only when he leaned over the plate with a cheap cigar: sulphur from the smoke turned the silver into black silver sulphide. The physicists Friedrich and Herschbach repeated the cigar trick in 2003 — it works (an anecdote, but a tested one).
On an assistant’s salary Stern smoked cheap cigars with a high sulphur content — and that is what saved the experiment. — after Friedrich and Herschbach, Physics Today (2003)
Spin: a foolishness the young can afford

In 1925 Uhlenbeck and Goudsmit proposed that the electron has an intrinsic angular momentum ±ħ/2. When Lorentz calculated that the electron’s “surface” would spin faster than light, they wanted to withdraw the paper — Ehrenfest had already sent it. Pauli was against it at first (he had talked Kronig out of the same idea). Phipps and Taylor (1927) repeated the Stern–Gerlach experiment with hydrogen atoms and confirmed that the two spots come from electron spin.
“You are both young enough to be able to afford a stupidity.” — Ehrenfest to Uhlenbeck and Goudsmit, 1925
A sphere before the qubit

Optics knew the same sphere: Poincaré (1892) mapped every polarisation of light to a point of a sphere — circular polarisation at the poles, linear on the equator. In 1927 Pauli wrote spin using three matrices σ<sub>x</sub>, σ<sub>y</sub>, σ<sub>z</sub>; their linear combinations are exactly the rotations of the Bloch sphere.
“Mathematics is the art of giving the same name to different things.” — Henri Poincaré
Nuclear induction and a geometric picture

In 1946 Bloch (Stanford) and Purcell (Harvard) independently discovered nuclear magnetic resonance in matter; they shared the Nobel Prize in 1952. Bloch described the motion of magnetisation as the rotation of a vector. Feynman, Vernon and Hellwarth (1957) showed that any two-level system can be drawn as an arrow in a ball — which is why we speak of the Bloch sphere of a qubit today.
Heisenberg: “Space is the field of linear operations.” Bloch: “Nonsense. Space is blue and birds fly through it.” — Bloch recalling a conversation with Heisenberg (Physics Today, 1976)
The word “qubit”

The word qubit was introduced by Benjamin Schumacher in the paper Quantum coding (1995) — reportedly as a joke from a conversation with William Wootters (it sounds like the biblical unit “cubit”). In the same paper he showed that the qubit is the unit of quantum information, just as the bit is the unit of classical information.
“The term ‘qubit’ was coined in jest during one of the author’s many intriguing and valuable conversations with W. K. Wootters.” — Schumacher, Quantum coding (1995)
Two slits and feeble light

Young (lectures 1801–1803 at the Royal Society) showed fringes behind two slits and thus the wave nature of light — against Newton’s authority. Taylor (1909) repeated the interference with light so feeble that on average less than one photon was inside the apparatus at a time; the exposure took three months and the fringes remained.
“The experiments I am about to relate … may be repeated with great ease, whenever the sun shines.” — Thomas Young, 1803
Electrons one at a time

Jönsson (1961) was first to perform the double-slit experiment with electrons. Merli, Missiroli and Pozzi (Bologna, 1974) and Tonomura (Hitachi, 1989) sent electrons one at a time: each lands as a dot, yet thousands of dots build up fringes. In 2002 the readers of Physics World voted it the most beautiful experiment in physics.

“A phenomenon which is impossible, absolutely impossible, to explain in any classical way, and which has in it the heart of quantum mechanics. In reality, it contains the only mystery.” — Feynman, 1965
The density matrix and decoherence

The density matrix was introduced independently by von Neumann and Landau (1927) to describe mixtures and subsystems. Zeh (1970) noticed that macroscopic systems cannot be isolated from their environment, and Zurek (1981–82) showed how the environment selects a “pointer” basis and wipes out coherences. Haroche and colleagues measured decoherence “live” in the lab (1996).
“Quantum theory is the only one we have; decoherence shows why the world looks classical to us.” — a paraphrase of W. Zurek’s idea
A Poisson bracket on a walk

In the summer of 1925 the 23-year-old Dirac received the proofs of Heisenberg’s paper. On a Sunday walk he realised that the commutator xp − px corresponds to the classical Poisson bracket — but the library was closed on Sunday, so he had to wait until Monday to check the formula. In 1930 he published The Principles of Quantum Mechanics; he added the bra-ket notation in 1939.
“It is more important to have beauty in one’s equations than to have them fit experiment.” — Dirac, Scientific American, 1963
The equation that predicted antimatter

Dirac’s relativistic equation (1928) had solutions with negative energy. Eventually (1931) Dirac saw a new particle in them — the anti-electron. Anderson found it in cosmic rays in 1932 (the positron). Dirac shared the 1933 Nobel Prize with Schrödinger; he considered declining it because of the publicity, until Rutherford told him that declining would attract even more.
“That was not a question, it was a comment.” — anecdote: Dirac, after someone in a lecture said they did not understand the equation in the top right
Lines that split

Zeeman (1896) placed a sodium flame between the poles of an electromagnet and the spectral lines broadened, later split. Lorentz explained it at once by the motion of charged particles in the atom and estimated their charge-to-mass ratio from the splitting — at about the time Thomson discovered the electron (1897). Nobel Prize 1902. The so-called “anomalous” Zeeman effect was explained only by spin.
“How can one look happy when one is thinking about the anomalous Zeeman effect?” — Pauli, around 1923
Atoms listen to the radio

At Columbia University (1938) Rabi’s group sent a molecular beam through a static field and an oscillating radio-frequency field. At exactly the right frequency the spins flipped and the beam missed the detector — the first measurement of magnetic resonance. Nobel Prize 1944. Atomic clocks, NMR and MRI all grew out of the method.
“Who ordered that?” — Rabi on the discovery of the muon (1936), a particle nobody expected
An echo, an image of the body, and Shor in a test tube

Hahn (1950) discovered the spin echo — a π pulse reverses the dephasing and the lost signal comes back. Lauterbur (1973) and Mansfield turned NMR into imaging (MRI; Nobel Prize 2003). In 2001 a team at IBM and Stanford (Vandersypen, Chuang et al.) ran Shor’s algorithm in an NMR molecule with 7 nuclear spins and factored 15 = 3 × 5.
“The echo was an accident — pulses I applied for other reasons produced a signal that should not have been there.” — a paraphrase of Hahn’s recollection
God does not play dice?

In a letter to Max Born (1926) Einstein rejected the idea that nature is fundamentally random. In May 1935 the EPR paper appeared: “Can Quantum-Mechanical Description of Physical Reality Be Considered Complete?”. Bohr replied in October 1935 with a paper of the same title: one cannot speak of reality without the experimental arrangement.
“The theory says a lot, but does not really bring us any closer to the secret of the Old One. I, at any rate, am convinced that He does not throw dice.” — Einstein to Born, 4 Dec 1926
Verschränkung and spooks

In the summer of 1935 Schrödinger and Einstein exchanged letters about EPR. Schrödinger coined the word Verschränkung — entanglement — for the phenomenon, and in the same year also the cat in the box. As late as 1947 Einstein wrote to Born about “spooky action at a distance” (spukhafte Fernwirkung).
“I would not call that one but rather the characteristic trait of quantum mechanics, the one that enforces its entire departure from classical lines of thought.” — Schrödinger on entanglement, 1935
From an inequality to a Nobel Prize

Bell (1964, during a sabbatical in the USA) derived an inequality that every local hidden-variable theory must satisfy. CHSH (1969) adapted it for real instruments; Freedman and Clauser (1972) violated it for the first time. Aspect (1982) switched the analysers while the photons were in flight. In 2015 three teams (Delft, Vienna, NIST) closed the main “loopholes” simultaneously. Nobel Prize 2022: Aspect, Clauser, Zeilinger.
“But in 1952 I saw the impossible done.” — Bell on Bohm’s theory, which refuted von Neumann’s “proof” against hidden variables
Como and Solvay

In September 1927 at Como, Bohr presented complementarity for the first time; Heisenberg published the uncertainty principle the same year. A month later, at the 5th Solvay Conference in Brussels, Einstein proposed every morning at breakfast a thought experiment meant to beat the uncertainty principle — and by evening Bohr had found the flaw. At the 6th conference (1930) Bohr refuted Einstein’s “photon box” using Einstein’s own general relativity.
“Einstein, stop telling God what to do!” — Bohr (as recalled by witnesses of the Solvay Conference, 1927)
The thinkers in the hall

Kant: Critique of Pure Reason (1781). Noether: the theorem on symmetries and conservation laws, Invariante Variationsprobleme (1918) — in his 1935 obituary Einstein called her the most significant creative mathematical genius since the higher education of women began. Wittgenstein: Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus (1921), proposition 5.6 on the limits of language. Heisenberg: Physics and Philosophy (1958), the Gifford Lectures.
“What we observe is not nature itself, but nature exposed to our method of questioning.” — Heisenberg, 1958
Interpretations multiply

Von Neumann (1932) put “collapse” (projection) into the formalism, together with an alleged proof that hidden variables are impossible. Bohm (1952) got around it with a non-local pilot wave. Everett (1957, PhD thesis) proposed that no collapse happens at all (later the “many-worlds” interpretation). Mermin (1989) summed up many physicists’ attitude with a phrase often misattributed to Feynman.
“If I were forced to sum up in one sentence what the Copenhagen interpretation says to me, it would be ‘Shut up and calculate!’” — N. David Mermin, Physics Today, 1989

Welcome to the workshop, Little Psi. Edward Purcell — in 1946 I was one of the first to measure nuclear magnetic resonance. Here you will run an NMR machine with your own hands: the magnet, the transmitter, the RF coil and the receiver.

The magnet creates a steady field B₀ along the z axis (a permanent magnet of about 1 T in SpinQ). The spins precess at the Larmor frequency [[ν₀ = γB₀/2π]] — for a proton [[γ/2π = 42.577 MHz/T]]. You do not set this frequency with a knob: the field and the nucleus fix it. You tune the transmitter until it is in resonance with it.

In the transverse direction (the x axis, perpendicular to B₀) sits the RF coil. It is not fed a steady current — it gets short current pulses at the frequency νRF. They create a rotating field B₁ ⟂ B₀ and tip the magnetisation by the angle [[θ = γB₁τ]]. The pulse phase decides about which transverse axis it turns.

And the measurement? After a pulse the precessing transverse magnetisation itself induces a voltage in the same coil — the free induction decay (FID). Finally we will correct the inaccuracies every real machine has: a miscalibrated pulse and an inhomogeneous field.

90°<sub>y</sub>: the same angle, a different pulse phase — the magnetisation ended up at +x. The phase of the RF pulse picks the rotation axis in the transverse plane; that is how arbitrary single-qubit gates are built in NMR.

Only a sequence that leaves transverse magnetisation gives a signal: 90° → FID (and the echo). Without a pulse or after 180° nothing precesses in the transverse plane, so the coil has nothing to pick up. The measured signal is an expectation value of the whole ensemble, [[⟨σx⟩, ⟨σy⟩]].

A signal null with the magnetisation down: the true 180° pulse lasts {0} µs, so the 90° pulse is {1} µs. The coil delivered {2} % of the nominal B₁ — without calibration every “gate” would be off and the errors would add up in an algorithm.
